subject: Creativity
title: Brainstorming Is Broken: Why Groups Kill Ideas
description: A quick, practical guide to Brainstorming Is Broken: Why Groups Kill Ideas.

hook.text: Alex Osborn invented brainstorming in 1953, promising it would double creative output.

buildup.text: Groups brainstorming together produce fewer AND lower-quality ideas than the same number of people working.

discovery.text: Three killers: production blocking (waiting your turn), evaluation apprehension (fear of judgment), and social loafing.

twist.text: The fix: 'brainwriting.' Everyone writes ideas silently, then shares them.

climax.text: Amazon's Jeff Bezos banned brainstorming meetings. Instead, everyone writes a six-page memo read silently.

punchline.text: Brainstorming feels creative. Working alone actually IS creative.

quiz.question: Why does traditional brainstorming produce fewer ideas than individual work?
options: Production blocking, evaluation apprehension, and social loafing

details.summary: Traditional brainstorming, where groups shout out ideas freely, consistently produces fewer and lower-quality ideas than individuals working alone. Social loafing, evaluation apprehension, and production blocking all undermine the process that Alex Osborn popularized in 1953.
details.whyItMatters: Brainstorming is one of the most widely used and least effective creative techniques. Understanding why it fails allows teams to adopt better alternatives that actually work.
takeaways: Group brainstorming produces fewer ideas than individuals working alone
Social inhibition and production blocking reduce output
Brainwriting and nominal group technique outperform verbal brainstorming

faq.question: Why does brainstorming feel productive even when it is not?
faq.answer: Groups feel more productive because social interaction is energizing and ideas feel more validated when shared aloud. The illusion of productivity is powerful, but controlled studies consistently show that the same people produce more and better ideas working independently.

faq.question: What should teams do instead of brainstorming?
faq.answer: Use brainwriting where everyone writes ideas silently before sharing, or nominal group technique where individuals generate ideas alone then discuss them. Both methods preserve the benefits of group evaluation while eliminating social inhibition.
